planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; unlike drought-adapted catmints, this species wants consistent moisture and struggles in hot, dry sites.

directions: Native to damp mountain meadows in Japan, this upright catmint departs from its dryland cousins by thriving in consistently moist, humus-rich soil and tolerating more shade than Walker's Low or Six Hills Giant types. Sturdy, non-flopping stems carry dense spikes of soft blue-violet flowers from midsummer into fall above fresh green, aromatic foliage, and deadheading the spent spikes encourages continued rebloom. It is an excellent choice for a partially shaded border edge or a spot near a downspout or rain garden where standard catmints would sulk, and it draws bees steadily through its long bloom season. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Blue Moon Catmint (Compact Dense-Spiked Nerve Catmint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, as this compact species resents wet winter soil.

directions: Blue Moon forms a dense, bushy mound of narrow green leaves topped from early to late summer with tightly packed, dark lavender-blue flower spikes, noticeably more compact and uniform than seed-grown Nepeta nervosa. Its low, tidy habit suits the front of a border, rock garden, or container, and shearing back by about a third after the first flush of bloom encourages a strong rebloom into fall. It is drought tolerant once established and needs no staking, holding its shape through summer storms better than taller catmints. Bees work the flowers steadily throughout the long bloom season.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Summer Love Agastache (Long-Blooming Dark Pink Hummingbird Mint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential for winter survival since agastache crowns rot readily in wet, heavy soil.

directions: Summer Love produces densely packed spikes of rich dark pink flowers held on sturdy, upright stems above fragrant, gray-green foliage. Bred as part of a series selected for colorful bracts that hold their color rather than fading to brown as the true flowers finish, it delivers a notably longer season of visual interest than older agastache cultivars. It blooms from early summer well into fall and is a strong draw for hummingbirds and bumble bees. Give it lean, sharply drained soil in full sun and avoid winter wet, the same conditions its dryland relatives need to overwinter reliably.
sources: Terra Nova Nurseries plant introduction notes

common_name: Kudos Yellow Agastache (Compact Dwarf Hummingbird Mint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential for winter survival since agastache crowns rot readily in wet, heavy soil.

directions: A genetically dwarfed selection bred without growth regulators, Kudos Yellow carries dense, well-branched spikes of clear yellow flowers over aromatic foliage from late spring through fall. It is part of a compact hummingbird mint series bred for garden performance, showing good resistance to powdery mildew and a sturdy, upright habit that needs no staking. Its steady, long bloom season makes it a reliable nectar source for hummingbirds and bees. Give it lean, sharply drained soil and full sun, and avoid winter wet to help the crown overwinter successfully.
sources: Terra Nova Nurseries plant introduction notes

common_name: Poquito Butter Yellow Agastache (Dwarf Compact Hummingbird Mint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential for winter survival since agastache crowns rot readily in wet, heavy soil.

directions: One of the most compact hummingbird mints available, Poquito Butter Yellow packs dense spikes of buttery yellow tubular flowers onto a tight, bushy 10 to 12 inch plant, making it a natural fit for containers, small borders, and sidewalk strips where taller agastache would overwhelm the space. Fragrant, medium green foliage backs a long bloom season that runs from late spring through fall. It is heat and drought tolerant once established and draws hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies steadily. Give it lean, sharply drained soil and full sun, and avoid winter wet to help the crown overwinter successfully.
sources: Terra Nova Nurseries plant introduction notes

common_name: Purple Rooster Bee Balm (Deep Royal Purple Mildew-Resistant Bergamot)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; give it room to spread since it forms an expanding clump like most Monarda didyma selections.

directions: Purple Rooster was selected for the darkest, truest royal purple flowers among bee balm cultivars, borne in dense, globular heads atop rigid, self-supporting stems that rarely need staking. Its rough-textured, dull green leaves have shown outstanding resistance to the powdery mildew that disfigures many older bee balm selections in humid summer weather. Plant it in moist, fertile soil with good air circulation, where it blooms for weeks in mid to late summer and draws hummingbirds and butterflies in steady numbers. Divide the clump every few years in spring to maintain vigor and control its spread.

common_name: Scorpion Bee Balm (Tall Reddish-Purple Mildew-Resistant Bergamot)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moderately fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; give it room to spread since it forms an expanding clump.

directions: Scorpion is a tall, clump-forming bee balm bearing masses of glowing reddish-purple flowers in dense, globular heads resting above a whorl of decorative purple bracts, blooming for weeks from midsummer into early fall. It shows significantly better resistance to powdery mildew than older bee balm varieties, an important trait in humid climates. Plant it in moderately fertile, humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist, where it tolerates part shade better than many bee balm selections and still flowers heavily. Butterflies and hummingbirds visit its nectar-rich blooms throughout the long bloom season, and dividing the clump every few years in spring keeps it vigorous.

common_name: Cherry Pops Bee Balm (Sugar Buzz Series Compact Cherry-Red Bergamot)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; its compact habit needs less staking and less room to spread than taller bee balm cultivars.

directions: Cherry Pops packs brilliant cherry-red flower heads onto a compact, well-branched plant bred for the middle of the border rather than the back, staying under two feet tall without staking. Bred for superior resistance to powdery mildew alongside its bright, saturated color, it holds up cleanly through humid summers that disfigure many older bee balm cultivars. Plant it in moist, fertile, well-drained soil where hummingbirds and butterflies will visit its nectar-rich blooms from midsummer into early fall. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and a tidy, mounding form.

common_name: Grape Gumball Bee Balm (Sugar Buzz Series Compact Magenta Bergamot)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; its compact, gently spreading habit fits more easily into a mixed border than larger bee balm cultivars.

directions: Grape Gumball produces vibrant magenta flower heads on a compact, mounding plant selected for its gentle spreading habit and good resistance to powdery mildew. It stays under two feet tall and needs no staking, making it easier to place in a mixed border than taller, floppier bee balm selections. Plant it in moist, fertile, well-drained soil, where it blooms from midsummer into early fall and draws hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies steadily. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to keep the planting vigorous and tidy.

common_name: Blue Moon Bee Balm (Sugar Buzz Series Compact Lavender-Blue Bergamot)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; its compact habit needs less staking and less room to spread than taller bee balm cultivars.

directions: Blue Moon brought a genuine breakthrough to compact bee balm breeding, delivering lavender-blue flower heads held by attractive purple bracts on a plant that stays under two feet tall, a shorter habit than older cultivars offered in this color range. It shows above-average resistance to powdery mildew and blooms without staking from midsummer into early fall. Plant it in moist, fertile, well-drained soil, where hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies will visit its nectar-rich flowers steadily through the season. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.
